evidence.text: So let me just cap it up. I think what Phil is saying is that he’d be in at a lower number. Charles would be in at a lower number. I tell you, I’m in at a lower number.

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: Awesome. Well, I’m Jason Fox. I’m the founder of EarBuds. And the idea for EarBuds came actually in my last career. I played in the NFL for six years. Just recently retired a couple years ago. And it was during that time, I always had this same idea over and over again. And really the first time I thought of it we were opening with Carolina, I was warming up right next to Cam Newton, he was on the field.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Oh I love Cam Newton! I’m sorry. Go ahead.

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: He was about five feet away from me. He’s jamming, he’s getting the crowd into it. He’s just getting into the rhythm right before a game. And I said, man, there’s 85,000 people here. There’s millions more watching this game at home. Cam is an individual that has tens of millions of social media followers. Like, how many people would love to be in his headphones right now?

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Hmn.

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: It was the number one question asked at the last two Super Bowl media days. It’s the number one question asked around the Olympics. What are you listening to? Well, Earbuds has solved that. So we’ve partnered with Spotify and Apple Music, and so instead of just listening to music, we allow you to broadcast it, where other people can tune in live and listen along with you in complete synchronized real time.

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: You wanna see it? Cool.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: OK, so you're pulling out your phone. We’re looking at a screen, says stream your music.

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: Yep. This is the app. So these are all people live-listening to your music right now.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: So you’re scrolling through.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: Who’s listening to Drake?

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: If you hit listen along, you start, you start completely synchronized with them.

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: We got NBA, NFL, X Games. We got so many people interested in using our tech.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: But why EarBuds? As soon as I saw you, I’m like, wow, what kind of new earbuds are you?

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Right.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: Buds. Like buds. Buddies.

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: We’re ear buddies.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Oh, I’m slow. But I guess I thought you were making

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Earbuds.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Earbuds.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Is this another revenue stream for, like, a boxer walking into the ring, what is he listening to? You know how they write things on their body? They’ll sell anything to sell. Would they sell the ability to broadcast the music?

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: Influencers are always very forward thinking now and knowing that what that relationship they have with their following and being able to engage with their fans in a whole new way through music. We’ve had labels, music promoters, artists want to launch new content through influencers. And they can brokerage their own deals around that. Imagine being the first song on Tom Brady’s playlist right before the Superbowl. Or the Michael Phelps example. Or being on Kylie Jenner’s playlist.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: And so how do you make money?

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: One, is sponsored content. We’ve had so many brands reach out, want to be served as labels, wanting to push music -- venues, arenas. And then the next way is partnerships, revenue shares, licensing opportunities. The sports teams, the leagues, the other live streaming services. The next one is the data play behind this. There’s so much data around music. For example if The Rock was listening, you know, we could analyze his following, his listeners. And we can show you these are the types of genres that your followers, where they live, their demographics. We can help people retarget those people.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: So can you tell us where you are now? Are you measuring active users? Where you at? Give us some numbers.

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: Yeah. So we say we’ve soft launched. We put it on the app store because we wanted to test and iterate and see where we’re at. And we’ve learned a ton. And we’re gearing up for a launch.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: And how many monthly active users do you have now?

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: It varies. But plus or minus 5,000.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Can you tell us about the competitors?

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: You know, there’s, there’s Vertigo tried to do it. It flopped out. It’s changed founders several times. There’s another one called Eavesdrop. Eavesdrop’s kind of floundered.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Why? Why have these dropped out and why have they floundered?

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: They’re most of them, I don’t think, I think we’re the only agnostic one. And, you know, I don’t think they have the same tech. And, you know, they outsourced the technology, which is just not a very good user experience. And then they’ve also struggled to onboard talent in a meaningful way.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Do they have any good talent? Any notable influencers on those platforms?

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: Not that I’m aware of, no.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Why doesn’t Spotify shut you out and do this? I mean, this sounds so obvious. Why is Spotify missing this?

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: They don’t do it because of really two reasons. The biggest reason is it’s a crowded experience. They’re cutting out features left and right because there’s just too much. They’ve gone so much into podcasts and moods and everything else. There’s just too much content on one screen. And the other big reason behind it is the agnosticity of it. The winner of the social space will be agnostic. Whether you get your music from your coworker, your girlfriend or even your favorite athlete or celebrity, they might not have the same music service as you. They might have Apple Music, you have Spotify. And so they’ve noticed that it’s hard to do social right.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: But couldn’t one argue that Spotify is so popular, so pervasive, that they have enough?

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: No. Apple Music is gigantic.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Well. Okay, either one of them is so. They have so many users, that this would be a great feature even if they kept it within their own platform.

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: I would disagree with you. There’s a couple different ways I could go here. One I’ll say is Shazam, right. Shazam sold, I know Rich Riley the former CEO, I’ve got connected to him through EarBuds, and he said the reason why he was a winner is because, he said, I’m Switzerland. It doesn’t matter. Anybody can use this. He goes, the winner of the social space will be the same way.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: The winner of this space will have a moat, and the moat is really simple: who got the stars on and using it.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Tell us about your relationships with any professional sport associations or teams? Like the winner of this space will have a moat, and the moat is really simple: who got the stars on and using it. What’s your star acquisition strategy?

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: Well, it’s to show them.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Relationships.

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: How they can monetize it themselves, right.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: But. But.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: Because he played.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: He’s already.

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: Yeah. I mean I used to live with Rob, Rob Gronkowski when we trained for the draft. Like, I have a relationship.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Right. He played, he just had.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Okay, but, okay, but, how are you, walk us through the strategy. Because, I think it’s great. But take away from football for one second, let’s go basketball. Anywhere else. Or swimming. Or. What is your acquisition strategy to make this really big?

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: It, it’s really the relationships. I know, I know that may not be the answer you want to hear, but we have those relationships. I was just with Baron Davis the last two days and he said he could get every NBA player.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: So their interest in doing it is so that they can make some extra money?

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: Well, the number one thing is, is they can engage with their fans. And then if they can do that by making money along the way, that’s the bonus.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: And that’s why actually the host of the X Games reached out to us.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Oh my.

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: Because he said, Jason, I’ve, when me and all my snowboard buddies get to the top of the mountain, we all press play at the same time.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: He goes, we’ve been asked and we’ve been, so many brands, and TV sponsors and everybody else, want to make music a part of the experience and now we can do that because now we can tell all of our riders to listen.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: For sure. You’re not just going from one person to one person, it’s actually if you were to get Ironman, if you get the X Games that goes viral within, those are millions and millions and millions.

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: I really think this will be driven by influencers in the early stages. Like, our whole mindset is to get on the top tier people. And like and we have some big name investors. Baker Mayfield invested in our last round. Patrick Mahomes is coming in this round.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Oh yeah.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Tell us about your previous rounds and this round.

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: We did a small friends and family round in the early days when we were just building a beta product. We raised $630,000 from friends and family. And then last year we raised $1.5.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: At valuations?

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: The first one was at $3 million pre-money. And then the last one was at $8 million.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Pre?

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: Pre money.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: And currently what are you doing?

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: We’re raising $3 million on a convertible note.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: What’s the cap?

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: The cap is at $14.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: So how much have you raised of the $3 million?

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: We’re a little north of halfway.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: OK.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: This is a tough one for me. But I’m going to pass. And it’s basically only because of price. If you told me, Hey, we’re just kicking it off, we don’t have any commitments at 14, I’d say I was in if we could talk about a set of terms that I think are more appropriate for where you are. I don’t generally feel comfortable asking people to revisit that. But I really think you have some good insights here. I think the product’s going to work. And I think kickstart.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Would you revisit that?

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: I was going to ask you what you thought a valuation would be fair.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: Eight.

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: Eight.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Despite the early stage, at 8 I’m in.

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: I’m, I’m interested. Um.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: So let me just cap it up. I think what Phil is saying is that he’d be in at a lower number. Charles would be in at a lower number. I tell you, I’m in at a lower number.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Me too.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: We’re all in.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: I’ll do a half a million at 8.

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: Look, I came here because I recognize, you know, who each and every one of you are, and the power behind that. And I want strategic capital that can help us in other ways. I do feel like I need to talk to our existing investors.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: Of course.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Sure you would.

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: Because I, I, you know, I believe they have a voice in this as well.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Of course.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: Of course.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: I’ll tell you the thing I like most about it, is I think it’s very, I think it’s very hard to find untapped, unmet consumer needs. And I think the number of times I've seen just regular people sitting around all on earbuds or AirPods, the idea that everyone can listen to the same thing, or everyone could listen to what someone else is listening to.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Oh, I’d do it.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: This is an untapped, consumer need. And you don’t find those in consumer very often. It’s basically impossible, as you probably know, it’s basically impossible to raise money for anything in music. Because generally you get stuck in the morass of licensing and the labels.

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: Very true.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: This is unique.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: The thing that I think is quite impressive about your presentation is you have a very understated humble but confident way of talking about your business that for me, as someone who has unfortunately lost money on some companies in music, it’s very sober. And in a good way. And I think that’s really impressive that you’re able to take what’s oftentimes just a rathole, a sinkhole, whatever you want to call it, industry for an entrepreneur to go into and tease out a really good independent conflict-free way to thread the needle.

turns.speaker: Jason
turns.text: I think if I go back to our current investors and the people that committed to this round, obviously the people committed to this round will. But I think the question I would first get asked is, like, well, How much?

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: I would, look, we’re at the tail end of our current fund, we have a new one coming online soon. So it would probably be 50. But with an eye, with an eye toward doing more if we could.
